title: Interfaith friendship
hook: A Common Word, a Muslim letter to Christian leaders on love of God and neighbor

segments.voice: Yesterday, killing innocents, and the verse that counts one life as all mankind. Your line was every soul sacred. Did you stop to remember one person behind a number? Today, from the worth of a stranger to the friendship of one. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

"Come to an agreement between us and you." That's a line from the Qur'an, and it became the title of a letter. Not a treaty or a press release: a long, careful letter, written by Muslim scholars and addressed to Christian leaders by name, the Pope among them, along with the heads of churches East and West. It doesn't ask anyone to change their faith. It asks them to look at two commandments both sides already say out loud. Today, interfaith friendship, and a letter called A Common Word.
screen: `A LINE BECOMES A TITLE.` → `ADDRESSED BY NAME.` → `TWO COMMANDMENTS.`

segments.voice: Start with the verse the title comes from, Surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall: "Say: O People of the Scripture! Come to an agreement between us and you." People of the Scripture is the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians. The Arabic for that agreement is kalimatin sawa', a word held in common, level between two parties. The letter takes that phrase and asks: what word do we already share? Its answer is two loves. Love of God. And love of neighbor. On the Christian side, it quotes Jesus himself, from the Gospel of Mark, in the King James words: "thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart." And then: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." On the Muslim side it sets the Qur'an's call to love and remember God next to a hadith in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase, that none of you truly believes until he loves for his neighbor what he loves for himself. Notice what the letter doesn't do. It doesn't say the two faiths are the same. It doesn't ask anyone to agree on who Jesus is. It says: here is ground we both already stand on, so let's meet there, and live in peace. Some Muslims set another verse beside it, from Surah al-Hujurat: "We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Know one another. Not merge, not argue anyone out of anything. Know. Letters like this can sound lofty. But the word at the center of this one is the plainest there is: neighbor.
screen: `COME TO AN AGREEMENT.` · `LOVE OF GOD, LOVE OF NEIGHBOR.` · `COMMON GROUND, NOT SAMENESS.` · `THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet someone of another faith, first in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you know whose faith, or lack of one, differs from yours. A coworker. A neighbor. A classmate's parent. See their face. Then ask what you actually know about what matters to them. Maybe very little. Maybe you've never asked. Choose one honest, friendly question you could ask them this week. If you pray, you can hold them in mind as a neighbor. If you don't, simply hold the question. The bell holds the time.
Interfaith friendship. Meeting across faiths on shared ground, as in A Common Word, a Muslim letter to Christian leaders on love of God and love of neighbor. Today's word.
Your line: love of God and neighbor. Today, ask your question, and listen to the whole answer. Tomorrow, facing Islamophobia. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims take part in interfaith dialogue through letters like A Common Word, mosque open days, shared meals and community service with churches and synagogues, and some point to 3:64 and 49:13 when they explain why.

fork.setup: you're writing a letter from Muslim scholars to Christian leaders. what do you build it on?
options: the differences, so nobody is confused.
two loves both already teach: love of God and love of neighbor.

fork.reveal: A Common Word builds on the two commandments, quoting the Gospel of Mark alongside the Qur'an and hadith, without claiming the faiths are the same.

original.note: Arabic: a word held in common, level between two parties (3:64); the letter's title.

trapdoor: what you thought: interfaith means pretending all religions are the same.
what it means: meeting on shared ground, love of God and love of neighbor, while each keeps its own faith.
what a scholar hears: 3:64's kalimatin sawa' as the title, Mark 12 set beside a hadith in Sahih Muslim, and 49:13's 'that ye may know one another' set beside it.

notes: The outline gives the year (2007); the script omits it and gives no count of signers, per the claims rule. Confirm 'addressed to Christian leaders by name, the Pope among them, along with the heads of churches East and West' against the letter's address list.
Confirm the letter's use of Mark 12 and of the Sahih Muslim 45 hadith (the letter cites the 'neighbor' wording).
Confirm Pickthall's wording for 3:64 and 49:13 exactly as quoted.
'People of the Scripture is the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians': confirm; some scholars extend the term.
The gloss of kalimatin sawa' as 'a word held in common, level between two parties' and the original-game spelling and transliteration need a check.
The carry is lowercase in the index ('love of god and neighbor'); the voice capitalizes God.

Editor: 49:13 was presented as sitting 'underneath it all', implying the letter rests on it; that is unverified, so it is now 'some Muslims set another verse beside it'. Cut the claim that letters like this 'end on' the word neighbor.
